title: The white days
tomorrow: they asked him about the moon. why did the answer mention doors?

cards: New year, new plan: run every single day, read every single night. A few weeks in, the plan is in pieces. In Medina, a companion named Abdullah ibn Amr makes a bigger vow.
He'll fast every day and pray all night, for as long as he lives. Word reaches the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, who comes to him and asks: is it true, what I've heard about you? Abdullah says yes.
So what does the Prophet tell him?

teach.h: FAST, AND EAT. PRAY, AND SLEEP.
teach.b: Not stop, and not more. In the reports in Sahih al-Bukhari, he tells him: fast, and also eat; pray, and also sleep. Your body has a right over you, your eyes have a right over you, your wife has a right over you.
Then he offers something smaller: three days each month. A good deed counts as ten, he says, so three days a month is like fasting all the time.
Abdullah pushes for more, and is given more, until he reaches the fast of Dawud: a day on, a day off. And here's the part to tell a friend tonight.
When Abdullah grew old, he said he wished he'd accepted the easier offer.
A report from Abu Dharr, in Jami' at-Tirmidhi, names them: the thirteenth, fourteenth and fifteenth of the lunar month.
They're known as al-ayyam al-bid, the white days, and tradition explains the name by the nights: around the full moon, they're bright enough to walk by. So the practice wasn't built for heroes.
It was handed to an eager man as the smaller, steadier option, and he spent his old age wishing he'd taken it. That's mid-month: three bright days, small enough to keep.

how: Some Muslims fast the 13th, 14th and 15th of each lunar month, the white days, eating before dawn and breaking the fast at sunset; lunar calendars and mosque announcements mark the dates.

o: three mid-month fast days, around the full moon

games.q: your friend vows to work out every single day this year, no rest days. you know Abdullah ibn Amr's story. what do you say?
o: start smaller and steady. your body has a right over you.
go all in. the bigger the vow, the bigger the reward.
don't bother. vows like that never last anyway.
games.why: the Prophet told Abdullah your body has a right over you, and offered three days a month. Abdullah, grown old, wished he'd taken it.

practice: Open whatever calendar you use and mark this month's middle three days, the thirteenth to the fifteenth of the lunar month; if you don't know the lunar date, mark the days around the next full moon.
Give them a small label: a fast, if you'll keep one, or one small thing set aside. The marking is the act.

wordCard.voice: The white days, al-ayyam al-bid: the thirteenth, fourteenth and fifteenth of each lunar month, with bright nights and a small fast.

orig.note: Arabic: al-ayyam al-bid, the white days; bid is the plural of abyad, white.

carryVoice: What stays with you: mid-month, three bright days, small enough to keep. A new part begins: the month and the year.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 1975 (Abdullah ibn Amr: fast and break, pray and sleep; your body, eyes and wife have a right over you; his wish in old age to have accepted the concession)
Sahih al-Bukhari 1976 (the vow to fast every day and pray every night; three days a month, a good deed counted as ten; the fast of Dawud)
Jami' at-Tirmidhi 761 (Abu Dharr: if you fast three days of the month, fast the 13th, 14th and 15th)
